newsitem.title: USA: Big Three May auto sales seen down from year ago.
newsitem.headline: Big Three May auto sales seen down from year ago.

text.p: The Big Three automakers are expected to report a down month for May light vehicle sales next week, but analysts say labour strikes against General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp. had a minimal effect on the decline.
Unit sales in the month are likely to be flat or down slightly, as the industry makes a modest recovery from a surprisingly weak April.
"We anticipate some bounce back, but not to the magnitude of what some people are anticipating," said Paul Ballew, chief economist for industry consultant J.D. Power and Associates.
Chrysler is expected to report results June 2, GM on June 3 and Ford Motor Co. on June 4.

Analyst estimates for May's seasonally adjusted annual sales rate range from 14 million units to 15 million units. The April rate was 14.3 million, the lowest seasonally adjusted rate since late 1995. The rate in May 1996 was 15.4 million.

Slow sales continued to plague Detroit's Big Three, according to Credit Suisse First Boston analyst Nicholas Colas. He predicts the group will be down 9.6 percent from May 1996, while Japanese automakers continue to chip away at the domestics' market share.

Chrysler will post the weakest results, Colas said, falling 17 percent from a year ago. Its passenger car sales continue to be poor, and Chrysler's normally hot-selling light trucks, the segment that includes minivans, pickup trucks and sport/utilty vehicles, could fall as much as 17 percent, Colas said.
GM is expected to report a 9 percent decline in total sales, predicted Burnham Securities Inc. analyst David Healy. Light trucks will be flat, but cars will fall 14 percent, he said.
Ford will make the best showing of the Big Three. Analysts said a modest increase in light truck sales will offset continued poor car demand for an estimated total company decline of about 5 percent.
"I don't think you can blame the strikes at GM and Chrysler for any great degree of those declines," said Healy.
He said both GM and Chrysler are up against strong year-ago comparisons. But their slumping sales also reflect the tough competitive environment.

Sales from imports and transplants will be down about 2 percent, Healy said. However, the group's market share continued to creep up, finishing May at an estimated 27.9 percent, compared with 27.6 percent for the first four months of 1997.

Ballew attributed some of the softness to capacity shortages among both the Big Three and Japanese automakers. He said some of the Japanese sales numbers may fall short of estimates because of extremely tight supplies of popular cars such as the Camry and Lexus ES 300 from Toyota Motor Corp., and the Civic from Honda Motor Co. Ltd.
"There are dealers screaming for inventory of those models and the product is just not in the pipeline," said Ballew.
